Comment: Devolution without discipline will just mean more tax

🕐 August 11, 2026
TW
Thomas Wexley
🐦 @Thomas_Wexley · Councillor and columnist
Listen to audio version of this article
Instaread
Sponsored by

Devolution, we are told, is the keynote policy of the new administration. Handing powers down to regional authorities sounds unimpeachable — who could object to decisions being taken closer to the people they affect? The trouble, as ever, is the bill.

Reorganising local government is a decades-old project that has limped along under governments of every stripe. Fewer layers can genuinely mean better value — but only if consolidation comes with spending restraint. Without it, bigger authorities simply acquire bigger appetites, and the easiest way to feed an appetite is a new precept on the council tax bill.

The pattern is familiar. A funding settlement is cut in the name of efficiency; the shortfall lands on local ratepayers in the name of local empowerment. Households in high-value areas are told they are the winners of devolution while their bills say otherwise. A mansion tax by another name is still a mansion tax.

None of this makes devolution a bad idea. It makes discipline the test. If new regional mayors arrive with hard spending caps, transparent accounts, and a legal bar on stealth levies, the reform deserves support. If they arrive with none of those things, taxpayers should read the small print — because they will be the ones paying for the large print.
